articles.title: She learned oil painting at a work offsite, and has painted sixty-eight Bible scenes since
articles.deck: Maria Clara works at Genpact, runs a household, and paints. Some canvases take six months. She talks about Daniel among lion-faced men, and why she calls it a mission rather than a hobby.

interviewMeta.subject: Maria Clara
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A Hyderabad-based painter who works in oils on biblical subjects. She has exhibited in churches, colleges and public auditoriums across the city, and blogs her work.

archiveMeta.editNote: First published as Talent Search #5. Reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected. One passage about a neighbour has been shortened at our discretion to keep a private third party out of it; Maria Clara's own account of her faith is unchanged.

body.v: Maria Clara is a painter in Hyderabad who works in oils on biblical subjects. Her paintings have been shown in churches, in public auditoriums and in colleges, and photographed for the press. When people ask her what a painting means, she tells them the story behind it. We were glad she gave us the time.
Where it started
5Talents: Hello Maria, greetings from 5Talents. How are you?
Greetings to you and to 5Talents readers in Jesus' name. Thank you for featuring me.
5Talents: When and how did you come to faith in Christ?

I come from a Roman Catholic background, and God in His grace had a plan for me and for my family. We got to know a neighbour who talked with us about Jesus, and as a family we began to want the word of God itself rather than the ritual around it. I received Jesus as my personal saviour on 5 November 1991, at a one-day retreat at Hebron Church, Golconda X Roads. I am married to Ch. Sushil Rao, a journalist with the Times of India, and we have a son, Ch. Nishan Sampreeth, in the tenth standard at Little Flower High School, Uppal.
5Talents: How and when did you discover your talent?

I strongly believe that nothing happens to His children by accident. In 2006 the company I work for, Genpact, ran a week's workshop in oil painting, glass painting and pottery, organised by Atiya Ahmed of Diaara Art Gallery in Banjara Hills. I joined the oil painting group and picked up the basics from an artist called Ashish.

The first few paintings had nothing to do with the Bible. Then one day I felt I should paint biblical subjects. We had friends coming to the house and we wanted to share the goodness of God with them, and sometimes it was difficult to bring the topic up. That was when I realised I could paint the incidents instead.
Through the paintings, we share the word of God.
body.highlight: we share the word of God

body.v: Daniel among men with the faces of lions
5Talents: How has Christ inspired your art?

Jesus is the central theme of all my paintings. The idea behind every one is to tell the gospel — how He died on the cross for our sins and rose again. I had only basic knowledge of painting, and it is the Lord who has guided me in creating the work. “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

I attend The King's Temple, and the teaching there each week gives me ideas that can be put on canvas. But it is usually only after my own experience of God in a particular situation that a new painting comes.

There is one of Daniel in the lions' den. It is a contemporary oil painting, and it shows human beings with the faces of lions. Daniel is relaxed among them. In ordinary situations there are people who might want to harm us, and when we trust God we can be that relaxed, and He will shut the mouths that are against us.

Another is of the widow in the Bible whose small jar of oil is poured out into vessel after vessel and does not run dry. She obeyed the prophet, and she saw the miracle. I have painted sixty-eight incidents from the Bible so far.
Exhibitions, and a blog
5Talents: How do you reach more people with your work?

I have held several exhibitions. Andhra Christian Theological College in Hyderabad organised a three-day one in August 2011, and more than three hundred people came through it. I was able to explain the miracles of God and His love through the paintings to a good many visitors who were not Christians. The artists P. Solomon Raj of Vijayawada and Jyoti Sahi of Bangalore both visited the gallery at my home in Nagole, which honoured me greatly.

There was another exhibition organised for United Nations World Women's Day at Hari Hara Kala Bhavan in 2011. The artist P. Narender Reddy invited me to exhibit alongside him at Taj Deccan in Banjara Hills, where I was able to explain the paintings to the chief minister and to the civil supplies minister. I have also shown the work at CSI Wesley Church, Musheerabad.

I keep a blog as well, and a few hundred people from around the world have visited it and written to me. A visitor from Spain asked to use some of the paintings in a book he was writing. Aradhana TV ran an hour-long programme about the work.
Six months on one canvas
5Talents: What has the Lord taught you through your talent?
I surrender every idea for a painting to God, and it is through Him that I create each work.

There are paintings I have worked on for about six months. God has taught me to persevere and to be disciplined. At times I have had to redo a painting completely because of a wrong combination of colour, or a wrong stroke, or because the painting itself was wrong. My office work keeps me busy, but with determination I take the time to work on them. All of them have a purpose, a reason and a meaning.
5Talents: What would you say to someone who is talented but sad, because they are not given the opportunity, or the talent is not recognised?

I work at Genpact and I take care of my family, and I still take out time to paint. It is not a hobby or a pastime. It is a mission. One should make a beginning and do what God has put in your heart. It is for God to open doors, and He will use every talent you have for His glory.
5Talents: And to someone who says, “I am not very talented — how could God use me?”

God has a plan for each one of us, and He made it before He laid the foundations of the earth. You need the urge to do something for God, and He will teach you how to do it. “Call to me and I will answer you and tell you great and unsearchable things you do not know.” (Jeremiah 33:3) He who made the heavens and the earth will give us knowledge, ideas, resources and favour to be used for Him. The Bible also says we are like clay jars in which this treasure is stored, and that the real power comes from God and not from us (2 Corinthians 4:7). God will use us if we let Him work through our weaknesses.
5Talents: Anything else for our readers?
God has blessed each of us with talents. Use them for Him. Nothing you do will go in vain.

articles.title: She could recite eighteen thousand verses of Sanskrit, and used it to argue for widows
articles.deck: Pandita Ramabai was orphaned by famine at sixteen, widowed at twenty-three, and went to England to train as a doctor. Deafness ended that. What she built instead at Kedgaon is still open.

archiveMeta.editNote: The 2012 version of this piece was not original work and has been replaced. This is a new article, written from Ramabai's own book and from scholarly reference sources listed at the foot.

body.v: This piece first ran in our October 2012 issue. That version was not our own writing and has been replaced. What follows is new work, researched from Ramabai's own book and from scholarly sources, listed at the end.

Her father taught her Sanskrit, which was not done. Girls were not given the sacred language, and men who taught it to their wives and daughters were despised for it. He was, and the family paid for it.

By her twenties she could recite the Puranas from memory in Sanskrit and discuss the grammar. When she reached Calcutta in 1878 the pandits examined her, could not fault her, and gave her the titles Pandita and Sarasvati. She was twenty. It is roughly as if a woman had been handed an honorary chair by the faculty that had spent a century refusing to admit her.
She spent the rest of her life using that authority against the people who had granted it.
A childhood spent walking

Ramabai Dongre was born in 1858. Her father, Anant Shastri Dongre, was a professional reciter — he travelled from village to village performing the epic and mythological texts for people who could not read them, and was paid in donations and gifts by listeners who believed merit came from hearing the words. He had married a nine-year-old girl when he was forty. He taught her Sanskrit too.

So the family walked. Hundreds of miles on foot, from temple to fair to wealthy household, living on what the recitations brought in. They never begged and never took other work. For years it was enough.

Then in 1874 the famine came, and it was not enough. They ate wild leaves and berries. Her father died of hunger, and within months so did her mother, and a sister as well. Ramabai was sixteen. She and her brother Srinivas kept walking and kept reciting, because it was the only trade they had.
Widowed at twenty-three

Srinivas died in 1880. She was alone at twenty-two, and by then she had joined the Brahmo Samaj, the reformist association that was arguing for exactly the things her life had made urgent — women's education, an end to child marriage, the treatment of widows.

In June 1880 she married Bipin Behari Medhavi, a Bengali lawyer. He was of much lower caste than she was, and the marriage was a scandal to everyone who knew her. Their daughter Manorama was born in April 1881. Less than a year later he died of cholera.

At twenty-three she was a high-caste widow with a baby, which in 1882 was among the worst positions a woman in India could occupy. A widow had no place in her husband's house. She was frequently blamed for his death, her head might be shaved, her food restricted, and she could expect to be treated as a household servant at best. Ramabai had spent her adolescence watching girls of eight and nine married off and then abandoned into that.
She had also, some time before, found a copy of the Gospel of Luke in her husband's library, in Bengali, and read it through.
The book that made her famous

She went to Pune, learned English, and started to write. In 1883 she sailed to England — to train as a doctor. That is the detail most retellings leave out, and it is the one that shows what she thought she was doing. She was not going abroad to be looked after. She intended to come back qualified.

She was going deaf, and the deafness ended the medical training. She stayed anyway, studied and lectured on social reform and education, taught Sanskrit at Cheltenham, and in 1883 was baptised at the chapel of an Anglican community at Wantage, whose sisters she had first met in Pune. She had been reading Nehemiah Goreh, an Indian theologian, and had come to the conclusion that what she valued in Brahmo thinking had come from Christianity in the first place.

Then she went to America, and in 1887 published The High-Caste Hindu Woman. It is an unsparing account of what her society did to its girls and widows, and it worked on readers because there was no way to dismiss the author as an outsider who had misunderstood. She had been the woman in the title.
American readers formed an association and promised her ten years of support. Ten years, she said, seemed like a lifetime.
body.attr: On the founding of the Ramabai Association, 1887

body.v: Sharada Sadan, and the rule she made
She came home and opened Sharada Sadan, the House of Learning, in Bombay in 1889, moving it soon after to Pune. It was a school for young widows, and it started with about twenty girls.

Here is the decision that deserves attention. Ramabai was by then a baptised Christian running a school funded by American Christians, and she made Sharada Sadan explicitly non-proselytising. The girls were not required to attend anything. Her supporters at home were nervous about it and her critics never believed it, and she held the line for years regardless.

She thought a widow of fifteen who had been given a bed, food and the alphabet was owed those things without conditions. Whatever else is true about her, she did not use what those girls needed as leverage, at a time when nobody would have stopped her.
Kedgaon

In 1896 and 1897 famine came again to central India. Ramabai, who knew precisely what was happening because it had killed her family, went out into it herself and brought back children — hundreds of them. She had bought land at Kedgaon, outside Pune, and in 1898 she opened Mukti there. The word means liberation.

At its height around two thousand women and girls lived at Mukti. It was not a dormitory. There was a school, a press, a hospital, workshops, oil presses, farmland and a weaving shed, and the older girls were trained first and then put in charge of teaching the younger ones. It was designed to produce women who could earn.

And she translated the Bible into Marathi. Not from an English version — she taught herself Hebrew and Greek in her sixties and worked from the original languages, setting the type at her own press. She was still finishing it when she died.
What it cost

Her health was bad for most of her adult life and much of Mukti's daily running fell to other people. The deafness never left. She was attacked from every direction at once: by orthodox opinion for abandoning her religion and her caste, and by some of her Christian supporters for refusing to convert the girls in her care and for being too Indian in how she ran things.
Manorama, her daughter, the child born in that eleven-month marriage, grew up to help run Mukti and died in 1921 at forty. Ramabai died nine months later, on 5 April 1922, aged sixty-three.
Why she is still known

India put her on a commemorative stamp for her contribution to the advancement of women. She is taught in Indian schools as a social reformer, which she was, and she is claimed by the Indian church, which she also was, and the two accounts of her rarely mention each other.
The Mukti Mission at Kedgaon is still open, and has been for more than a hundred and twenty-five years.
So what, in 2026?

She was extremely good at one specific, difficult, useless-looking thing. She could handle Sanskrit at a level almost no one could, in a language that earned nothing and was withheld from her by custom. She could not have known it would matter.

It turned out to be the whole lever. The scholarship got her the title, the title got her the platform, the platform got her the book, the book got her the funding, and the funding built Kedgaon. A woman with the same convictions and no Sanskrit would have been ignored.

If you are seventeen and being told that what you are good at is impractical, she is a reasonable argument for learning it properly anyway. Not because it will pay. Because when you finally have something to say, the difference between being listened to and being dismissed is usually whether you are undeniably good at something first.

Sources: Pandita Ramabai, The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887), available at Archive.org; Eric J. Sharpe, “Ramabai, Dongre Medhavi”, in the Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions, ed. Gerald H. Anderson (1998), via Boston University School of Theology's History of Missiology; Nicol Macnicol, Pandita Ramabai (1926); A. B. Shah, ed., The Letters and Correspondence of Pandita Ramabai, compiled by Sister Geraldine (1977); the Ramabai Mukti Mission's own records.
